timing_gold.source: observed — D7, MuckRock aggregate statistics scraped 2026-09-15: San Francisco Police Department 157 days, City and County of San Francisco (general/citywide) 128 days. Statutory and ordinance ceiling for comparison: 24 days (10 + 14), or next business day for an Immediate Disclosure Request.
timing_gold.quote: Success rates cluster around 32% for the three police/law-enforcement agencies but jump to 75% for the general city agency, suggesting the gap between statute and practice is concentrated in law-enforcement records specifically.

timing_gold.note: Both figures are MuckRock means over all request types, not medians, and they measure the records-request leg only. No observed duration exists for either appeal step.

known_gaps: Whether the appeal track is ever actually used, and how long it actually takes. The Supervisor of Records 10-day deadline and the SOTF 45-day deadline are precisely written, but this corpus recovered no timed instance of either step — no petition-to-determination duration, no complaint-to-order duration, no compliance rate for SOTF orders.

Whether SOTF orders produce records. D1 specifies five-business-day compliance, committee monitoring and referral to the DA/AG/Board/Ethics Commission, but nothing states how often non-compliance is referred or what any referral has ever produced. A first-person account from a sitting SOTF member (reddit, user-report tier) describes the body as toothless, directly contradicting the procedural confidence of D1.

The Immediate Disclosure Request is the sharpest designed-vs-observed gap in the whole corpus: the ordinance's fastest track (next business day) produced the single worst observed outcome (6+ years, ~60 ignored follow-ups). No document explains what happens to an IDR that is simply not answered, or who is supposed to notice.

SF's internal routing. D1 and D2 describe the appeal machinery in fine grain but say almost nothing about the custodian side: no SF equivalent of LAPD's CPRA Unit Manual was located, so the department-level intake, search, exemption-review and redaction workflow (A03–A09 here) is reconstructed from the ordinance plus observed request logs, not from an SF SOP.

Which exemptions SF departments actually invoke, and how often. Observed samples show SFPD asserting investigative-records exemptions over both open and closed files and routing complaint records to the Department of Police Accountability, but no SF document enumerates its own exemption practice.

Fee practice versus the caps. The ordinance caps routine copies at a cent a page, yet SFPD's observed MuckRock average fee is $94.30. Nothing in the corpus reconciles the two — whether through the 'custom copies' rate, an itemized cost analysis, or the state's electronic-record construction provisions.

Retention upstream of the request. One sampled SFPD response states lobby camera footage was already gone under a 10-day retention rule; no SF retention schedule is held in the corpus, so which records expire before a 10-day determination is even due is unknown.
notes: San Francisco is the corpus's clearest case of a local rule building on a state statute: it keeps the state's 10-day determination but adds three things the state has none of — the next-business-day Immediate Disclosure Request (A02), hard fee caps far below 'direct cost' (A08), and a free two-tier administrative appeal (A10 Supervisor of Records, then A11–A24 SOTF) where the state's only remedy is litigation. For SF the declared and local-rule tiers collapse into the same documents: no clean SF applicant-facing program page was recoverable (sf.gov's public-records page 404'd at fetch time), so the ordinance text and the SOTF procedure ARE the applicant-facing documents. That is why relatively few activities here are marked staff_only (6 of 27): almost everything in the appeal track is written down in a document aimed at complainants. The staff_only calls are the completeness screen (A13), the priority-calendaring mechanic (A15), the Deputy City Attorney memorandum (A17), the combine/cap docket rules (A19), compliance monitoring (A22), the table/close-for-inactivity power (A25) and the petition log (A26) — the docket-management machinery, which is exactly the part that determines whether a complaint is ever heard. IMPORTANT CAVEAT for scoring: D2 is a fetch-tool extraction of the ordinance page, not a raw text dump, so quotes attributed to D2 are verbatim to the saved file and to the fragments that file itself marks as quoted; re-verify any D2 quote against the ordinance text before treating it as load-bearing. SFPD is used as the worked custodian because that is where the observed data is; the model is otherwise citywide.
